title: Finding an English-Speaking Counsellor When You Live Abroad
excerpt: Why working in your own language matters, and how to find counselling support that fits an international life.

value.text: You have built a life in a new country. You order coffee in the local language, you navigate the paperwork, you have found your way around. And then something in your inner world needs attention — a stretch of stress, a loss, a growing sense of disconnection — and you realise you want to talk to someone who truly understands you. In English. That instinct is not a weakness. It is one of the most important things you can honour.
Living abroad is rich and expanding, but it can also be quietly demanding. When you go looking for support in those moments, the language you speak matters far more than people expect.
Why your own language matters so much

Emotion lives in language, and usually in the language you grew up with. You can be perfectly fluent in a second language for work and daily life, and still find that your feelings do not translate. The precise word for a particular ache, the phrase your grandmother used, the way you naturally reach for humour or metaphor — these live in your mother tongue.

In counselling, that precision is not a luxury. It is much of the work. When you have to translate your inner life before you can share it, part of your attention goes to the translating rather than the feeling. Working in English — or whichever language is truly yours — lets you drop that extra layer and simply say what is real, in the words that fit.
The particular weight of building a life abroad

There is also the content of what you may want to talk about. Much of it is bound up with being international: homesickness that surprises you, relationships stretched across distance, the strange grief of missing a home you also chose to leave, the effort of belonging in two places at once and sometimes feeling fully at home in neither.

A counsellor who understands international life does not need all of this explained from scratch. That shared understanding lets you get to what matters more quickly. If any of this resonates, you may find [built a life abroad but it doesn't feel like home](/blog/built-a-life-abroad-not-at-home) speaks to it directly. Working in your own language, with someone who knows the terrain, can be a real relief.

The good news is that living abroad no longer limits you to whoever happens to be nearby. Online counselling means you can work with someone whose language and approach genuinely fit, wherever you both are. You are no longer choosing between the local counsellor who does not share your language and no support at all.

It also brings a welcome continuity. If your international life involves further moves, an online counsellor can stay with you across them — one steady relationship while the geography around you keeps shifting. For many people that stability is exactly what they most need.
As you search, a few things are worth weighing up beyond language alone:

items: Someone who understands the international, cross-cultural experience from the inside, not just in theory.
An approach that fits what you are carrying — for stress, overwhelm, and life transitions, a warm and practical counselling style tends to serve well.
Comfortable, secure online working, so distance and time zones are not an obstacle.
A relationship that feels right to you — which usually only becomes clear in a first conversation.

value.text: I offer counselling online, internationally, in both English and German, and I know the terrain of international life from my own experience. You can read more about my background on my [about page](/about) or explore how sessions work on the [work together page](/work-with-me).

If you have been quietly wishing for someone who simply gets it — in your own words — that wish is worth acting on. You are welcome to [get in touch](/contact) whenever you feel ready. Reaching out in your own language, to someone who understands, can be the moment things start to feel a little lighter.
